import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components'

This page is for an Express API that needs sign-in and is about to grow a hand-written JWT helper.
`@seamless-auth/express` replaces that helper. It mounts the `/auth` routes the frontend SDKs call,
keeps the session in signed `HttpOnly` cookies on your own domain, and gives you `requireAuth`, a
middleware that answers `401` without a session and puts the signed-in user on `req.user`. Sign-in
itself (passkeys, magic links, email and SMS one-time codes, OAuth) runs on a Seamless Auth server:
self-hosted [`seamless-auth-api`](/build/auth-api) or a managed instance.

**Why not write the 40 lines yourself?** Signing a token is the easy part. The work is everywhere
around it: where the token lives in the browser so a script cannot read it, refresh that rotates
without logging people out across tabs, revoking a session that has been stolen, and the passkey
(WebAuthn) ceremonies, which no JWT helper covers. The adapter and the auth server do all of that.
The Express adapter is the reference implementation: the other adapters are tested against its
responses.

Versions on this page: `@seamless-auth/express` 0.20.0 (Express 5), `@seamless-auth/react` 0.16.0,
`seamless-cli` 0.22.0. All are pre-1.0.

---

## Fastest Path: A New Project

One command, no prompts, safe for scripts and agents:

```bash
npx seamless-cli init my-app --local --yes --email=you@example.com
cd my-app
docker compose up
```

This scaffolds a React web app on `http://localhost:5173`, an Express API on
`http://localhost:3000` with this adapter already wired in, the auth server in Docker, and the
admin console at `http://localhost:3000/console`. Register with the email you passed and that
account becomes the first admin. The [Self-Hosted Quickstart](/start/quickstart) walks through it.

---

## Add It To An Existing Express App

<Aside type="tip">
  `npx seamless-cli add --local --email=you@example.com`, run in your project, does steps 1 and 2
  for you and prints step 3: it finds your Express app (at the root or in `api/`, `server/`,
  `backend/`, `apps/*`, or `packages/*`, among others), writes a local auth server to
  `seamless/`, writes the values below into your `.env` without touching ones you already have,
  installs the packages, and prints the code to paste. It never edits your source files. Use
  `--app <id>` instead of `--local` for a managed application. See
  [Add Seamless Auth To An Existing App](/operate/add-to-existing-app).
</Aside>

### 1. Have An Auth Server

Either run one locally (`seamless add --local` above writes `seamless/docker-compose.yml`; start
it with `docker compose -f seamless/docker-compose.yml up -d`), or create a managed application in
the portal ([Managed Quickstart](/start/managed-quickstart)). You need its URL and its service
token.

### 2. Install

```bash
npm install @seamless-auth/express cookie-parser cors
npm install -D @types/cookie-parser @types/cors
```

`@seamless-auth/express` needs Express 5 and Node.js 22 or later.

### 3. The Server

This is a complete server: it mounts `/auth`, protects three routes, and reads the user. It is
the shape the Express starter in `seamless-templates` uses, trimmed to the auth parts.

```ts
// server.ts
import express from 'express'
import cookieParser from 'cookie-parser'
import cors from 'cors'
import createSeamlessAuthServer, {
  getSeamlessUser,
  requireAuth,
  requireRole,
  type SeamlessAuthMessagingOptions,
  type SeamlessAuthServerOptions,
  type SeamlessAuthUser,
} from '@seamless-auth/express'

declare global {
  namespace Express {
    interface Request {
      user?: SeamlessAuthUser
    }
  }
}

// Development only: print one-time codes and magic links to this console instead
// of sending them, so you can sign in with no mail or SMS provider.
const devMessaging: SeamlessAuthMessagingOptions = {
  handlers: {
    sendOtpEmail: async ({ to, token }) => {
      console.log(`Dev code for ${to}: ${token}`)
      return { accepted: true, provider: 'console', channel: 'email' }
    },
    sendOtpSms: async ({ to, token }) => {
      console.log(`Dev code for ${to}: ${token}`)
      return { accepted: true, provider: 'console', channel: 'sms' }
    },
    sendMagicLinkEmail: async ({ to, magicLinkUrl }) => {
      console.log(`Dev magic link for ${to}: ${magicLinkUrl}`)
      return { accepted: true, provider: 'console', channel: 'email' }
    },
  },
}

// Set AUTH_SERVER_ISSUER only when the auth server signs as a different URL from
// the one this API calls, as the local Docker stack does (http://auth:5312).
const issuer = process.env.AUTH_SERVER_ISSUER || undefined

const auth: SeamlessAuthServerOptions = {
  authServerUrl: process.env.AUTH_SERVER_URL!,
  authServerIssuer: issuer,
  audience: issuer ?? process.env.AUTH_SERVER_URL!,
  cookieSecret: process.env.COOKIE_SIGNING_KEY!,
  serviceSecret: process.env.API_SERVICE_TOKEN!,
  jwksKid: process.env.JWKS_KID,
  messaging: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production' ? undefined : devMessaging,
}

const app = express()

// The web app calls /auth on this server with cookies, so CORS must allow credentials.
app.use(cors({ origin: process.env.UI_ORIGINS?.split(','), credentials: true }))
app.use(express.json())
app.use(cookieParser())

// Every route the frontend SDK calls: passkeys, magic links, OTP, refresh, logout.
app.use('/auth', createSeamlessAuthServer(auth))

// requireAuth answers 401 unless the request carries a valid session cookie.
const signedIn = requireAuth({ cookieSecret: auth.cookieSecret })

app.get('/api/me', signedIn, (req, res) => {
  res.json({ id: req.user!.id, roles: req.user!.roles })
})

// The full profile (email, phone, last login) comes from the auth server.
app.get('/api/profile', signedIn, async (req, res) => {
  res.json(await getSeamlessUser(req, auth))
})

app.get('/api/admin', signedIn, requireRole('admin'), (_req, res) => {
  res.json({ ok: true })
})

app.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000))
```

Run it with `npx tsx --env-file=.env server.ts`. In plain JavaScript, drop the `declare global`
block and the type imports; nothing else changes.

- The one line that adds auth is `app.use('/auth', createSeamlessAuthServer(auth))`. The one
  line that protects a route is `requireAuth({ cookieSecret })`.
- Without a session, `requireAuth` answers `401 { "error": "Failed to find authentication token
  required" }`, and `401 { "error": "Invalid or expired session" }` for a cookie that does not
  verify. `requireRole` answers `403` when the user lacks the role. Scoped roles work as described
  in [How To Secure Routes](/build/secure-routes).
- `req.user` is what the session cookie carries: `id`, `roles`, and usually `email` and `phone`.
  It is read locally, with no network call. `getSeamlessUser(req, auth)` asks the auth server for
  the full profile.
- `requireAuth` never refreshes. An expired access cookie is renewed by the frontend SDK through
  `/auth`, which the adapter handles.
- To accept the auth server's access token as `Authorization: Bearer` too (for a native app), pass
  `authServerUrl` and `audience` to `requireAuth`; see
  [Bearer Transport](/build/server-sdks#bearer-transport-for-native-clients).

### 4. Environment Variables

For an API run on the host against the local Docker stack:

```bash
# .env
AUTH_SERVER_URL=http://localhost:5312
AUTH_SERVER_ISSUER=http://auth:5312
API_SERVICE_TOKEN=the-auth-servers-API_SERVICE_TOKEN
COOKIE_SIGNING_KEY=output-of-openssl-rand-base64-48
JWKS_KID=dev-main
UI_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5173
```

| Variable             | What it is                                                                                                                                                        |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `AUTH_SERVER_URL`    | The Seamless Auth server this API calls. For a managed application, the Auth Server URL from the portal                                                           |
| `AUTH_SERVER_ISSUER` | Only for an API run on the host against the local Docker stack, which signs as `http://auth:5312`. Leave it unset otherwise                                        |
| `API_SERVICE_TOKEN`  | The secret shared with the auth server, 32 characters or more. Locally, the auth server's `API_SERVICE_TOKEN`; managed, a service token generated in the portal     |
| `COOKIE_SIGNING_KEY` | Signs the session cookies, 32 characters or more. Generate it with `openssl rand -base64 48`                                                                      |
| `JWKS_KID`           | Key id on the service tokens the adapter signs. The local stack uses `dev-main`; the adapter warns while it is `dev-main`, so set your own in production          |
| `UI_ORIGINS`         | Comma-separated web origins allowed by CORS                                                                                                                        |

The adapter refuses to start when either secret is shorter than 32 characters. Cookie options
(`cookieDomain`, `cookieSecure`, `cookieSameSite`, custom cookie names) are in
[Server SDKs](/build/server-sdks#required-options), and the starter's variables in
[Environment Variables](/reference/environment-variables#starter-environment).

### 5. The Frontend

The React SDK talks to `/auth` on your API and ships the sign-in screens:

```bash
npm install @seamless-auth/react react-router-dom
```

```tsx
// src/App.tsx
import { BrowserRouter, Route, Routes } from 'react-router-dom'
import { AuthProvider, useAuth, useAuthorizedFetch } from '@seamless-auth/react'
import { AuthRoutes } from '@seamless-auth/react/routes'

function Home() {
  const { user, logout } = useAuth()
  const authorizedFetch = useAuthorizedFetch()

  // A path starting with / goes to apiHost, with the session cookies attached.
  const loadMe = async () => console.log(await (await authorizedFetch('/api/me')).json())

  return (
    <main>
      <p>Signed in as {user?.email}</p>
      <button onClick={() => void loadMe()}>Call /api/me</button>
      <button onClick={() => void logout()}>Sign out</button>
    </main>
  )
}

function AppRoutes() {
  const { isAuthenticated, loading } = useAuth()
  if (loading) return null

  return (
    <Routes>
      <Route path="*" element={isAuthenticated ? <Home /> : <AuthRoutes />} />
    </Routes>
  )
}

export default function App() {
  return (
    <BrowserRouter>
      <AuthProvider apiHost={import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL}>
        <AppRoutes />
      </AuthProvider>
    </BrowserRouter>
  )
}
```

Set `VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:3000` in the web app's `.env`. `AuthRoutes` renders the
sign-in, registration, passkey, one-time code, and magic link screens, including the
`/verify-magiclink` page the emailed link opens. To build your own screens instead, see
[How To Build Your Own Auth UI](/build/custom-auth-ui). Vue, Svelte, Angular, and React Native have
their own SDKs ([Ecosystem](/build/ecosystem)).

The web app's origin also has to be in the auth server's `ORIGINS`, or passkey ceremonies fail.
The local stack already allows `http://localhost:5173`.

---

## What Not To Write Yourself

With the adapter mounted, delete or never write:

- JWT signing, verification, or a `jsonwebtoken` helper for sessions
- a `/login`, `/logout`, `/refresh`, or `/me` route of your own
- code that sets or clears auth cookies, or stores tokens in `localStorage`
- refresh-token rotation, reuse detection, or session revocation
- password hashing, reset emails, or a users table column for passwords
- WebAuthn challenge and attestation handling for passkeys
- one-time code or magic link generation, expiry, and rate limiting

Keep your own users table if you want one, keyed by `req.user.id`. The Express starter does this
with a `findOrCreate` on the first authenticated request.
